in_text_mentions: She was diagnosed with short-limbed dwarfism and her height was 118 cm (7.6 SD). She had short stubby trident hands and a concave facial profile was also noticed. Hyporeflexia of bilateral legs was detected, Babinski reflex was positive on both sides, and the patient could not sleep in the supine position due to severe thoracolumbar kyphosis. The patient had slight muscle weakness in her bilateral legs. The result for the manual muscle test (MMT) of her bilateral legs was 4 for both legs. (Figure 1A–C).

Radiograms at the initial visit demonstrated there was no scoliosis, but there was severe kyphotic deformity of the thoracolumbar area; T11–L2 local kyphotic angle was 76°, sagittal vertical axis (SVA) 55 mm, pelvic tilt (PT) 32°, and PI 52° (Figure 1D,E). Preoperative radiograms showed progression of kyphosis to be 126° (Figure 1F,G). Preoperative computer tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed wedged vertebra (T12 and L1) and stenosis at the thoracolumbar junction (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Radiograph of pelvis and femur showing classic achondroplasia features: narrow sacrosciatic notches (tombstone iliac wings) and femoral shortening (rhizomelic shortening) in a 3-year-old patient. B: Radiograph of lower legs showing distal overgrowth of the fibulae, a recognized feature of achondroplasia. C: AP radiograph of spine showing platyspondyly and interpediculate narrowing, classic radiographic features of achondroplasia. D: Lateral radiograph of spine showing narrow spinal canal and wedge vertebra at L2, characteristic findings in achondroplasia. E: PA radiograph of left hand showing significant brachydactyly and brachymetacarpia (trident hand), a classic manifestation of achondroplasia.

panels.figure_caption: Radiographs of a case of achondroplasia with a p.Asn540Lys mutation (R#00-347). (A) Pelvis and femur, age 3 years. Narrow sacrosciatic notches and femoral shortening. (B) AP lower legs, age 3 years. There is distal overgrowth of the fibulae. (C) AP spine, age 3 years, shows platyspondyly and interpediculate narrowing in the lumbar spine. (D) Lateral spine, age 3 years. Note a narrow spinal canal and a wedge vertebrae at L2. (E) PA, left hand, age 3 years. There is significant brachydactyly and brachymetacarpia.
in_text_mentions: Figure1 shows the radiographs for one of the patients with clinical ACH due to a p.Asn540Lys mutation (R#00-347). He was first seen at our center at 40 months of age. He was brought in by his adoptive parents who knew little of his prior history. Born at 32 weeks, he was diagnosed with ACH in the first year of life. His height was 85 cm (+2 SD on the ACH growth chart) and head circumference 53 cm (95%). He had macrocephaly, midface hypoplasia, rhizomelic shortening of the limbs, and brachydactyly typical for ACH. At his last visit, he was 11.5 years old and his height was 132.8 cm (+2.5 SD on
Radiographic findings, such as narrow spine canal, a wedge vertebrae at L2, (Fig.1D) and significant brachydactyly and brachymetacarpia, support a diagnosis of ACH.

She was delivered via elective cesarean section because of a breech presentation. Birth growth parameters were as follows: weight, 3,292 g (+1.6 standard deviation (SD)); length, 42 cm (−2.9 SD); and head circumference, 38 cm (+3.83 SD). Diagnosis was confirmed using genetic testing, which identified a heterozygous pathogenic variant of the FGFR3 gene (p.Gly380Arg).

in_text_mentions: ‐year‐old mother and a 34‐year‐old father. The Apgar scores were four and six at 1 and 5 min, respectively. She showed severe shortening of the upper and lower extremities with redundant skin folds, a small chest, frontal bossing, midface hypoplasia, and trident hands. Neonatal radiographs showed a small thorax with short ribs, abdominal distension (Figure 1a), hypoplastic ilium with narrow sciatic notch, proximal femoral radiolucencies, and metaphyseal cupping of the long tubular bones (Figure 1b). Based on these clinical and radiological characteristics, she was tentatively diagnosed as ACH.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels ((a), (b), (c), (d), (e)). (a): MRI shows hydrocephalus and foramen magnum stenosis, known complications of achondroplasia in infancy per article text. (b): Lateral skull radiograph demonstrates characteristic craniofacial dysmorphisms of achondroplasia including frontal bossing per article text. (c): Lateral spine radiograph shows platyspondyly and tongue-like vertebral protrusion typical of achondroplasia, with metaphyseal flaring of ribs. (d): Hand radiograph shows severe brachydactyly with metaphyseal cupping, characteristic trident hand appearance in achondroplasia. (e): Lower limb radiograph demonstrates extremely shortened thin long bones with deficient epiphyseal/metaphyseal ossification consistent with achondroplasia.

Metacarpals of both hands were short and of similar length with separation of middle and ring fingers (trident hand) (Figure 2).
